title.narrative: APHRC /Africa Population and Health Research Center SRHR 2024-2027
APHRC /Africa Population and Health Research Center SRHR 2024-2027

description.narrative:
Det övergripande målet är att bidra till en förbättrad användning och implementering av relevanta nationella, regionala och globala lagar och policyer om universell tillgång till rättmätiga SRHR-tjänster och social integrering av homo- och bisexuella, transpersoner, queera personer och personer med intersexvariation (HBTQI+). Projektförslaget är en fortsättning på Fas 1, som Sida finansierat mellan 2018–2024.
Projektet bygger på att tillvarata investeringar gjorda i Fas 1 och fokuserar på att öka policyåtaganden och implementering av SRHR-insatser i Afrika inom tre, mer omtvistade, områden: 1) ungdomars SRHR, 2) tillgång till säker och laglig abortvård och postabortvård, och 3) inkludering av HBTQI+ populationer. För att uppnå detta kommer APHRC att genomföra studier på vad som krävs för att förbättra SRHR (med fokus på de tre områdena), använda resultaten från dessa i sitt påverkansarbete gentemot beslutsfattare på nationell - och regional nivå men också för att stärka nyckelaktörers kapacitet att använda evidens för beslutsfattande om SRHR. Projektet är regionalt och har ett särskilt fokus på Kenya, Rwanda, Liberia, Sierra Leone, Burkina Faso, Benin, Zambia och Malawi.

The overall goal is to contribute to the improved use and implementation of relevant national, regional, and global laws and policies on universal access to legitimate SRHR services and the social inclusion of lesbian, gay, bisexual, queer and intersex (LGBTQI+) people. The project proposal is a continuation of Phase 1, which Sida funded between 2018–2024.
The new project is based on leveraging investments made in Phase 1 and focuses on increasing policy commitments and implementation of SRHR interventions in Africa in three, more contentious, areas: 1) adolescents’ SRHR, 2) access to safe and legal abortion care and post-abortion care, and 3) inclusion of LGBTQI+ populations. To achieve this, APHRC will conduct studies on what is required to improve SRHR (with a focus on the three areas), using the results from these in its advocacy work towards decision-makers at national and regional level, but also to strengthen key actors’ capacity to use evidence for decision-making on SRHR. The project is regional and has a special focus on Kenya, Rwanda, Liberia, Sierra Leone, Burkina Faso, Benin, Zambia, and Malawi.

Overall goal The overall goal is to contribute to the enhanced domestication and implementation of relevant national, subregional, regional and global laws and policies (including frameworks, instruments, protocols, treaties, and commitments) on universal access to comprehensive SRHR services and the social inclusion of LGBTQI groups.
Objectives 1) To generate and synthesize quality evidence to inform policies and programs related to the three contentious issues: i) access to safe and legal abortion and postabortion care (ii) adolescent SRHR and (iii) the (in)exclusion of LGBTQI groups. 2) To translate and strategically share evidence to inform policies and programs that seek to enhance access to safe and legal abortion and postabortion care, improve adolescent SRHR services, and enhance the social inclusion of LGBTQI people across SSA. 3) To strengthen the capacity of APHRC staff, partners, and policy actors to generate, translate and use evidence on contentious SRHR issues. 4) To cultivate and nurture partnerships with critical policy actors to enable the demand for the generation and uptake of evidence to inform SRHR policies and programs.

This contribution started in December 2024 and is a continuation of phase 1 of Challenging the Politics of Social Exclusion Project.
Some of the results achieved in 2025 include the following:
1. Improved access to SRHR information and services: CPSE is testing a mentorship-based post-abortion care and post-rape care quality improvement model in Kilifi County, in Kenya (20 mentors, 95 mentees), institutionalizing continuous skills transfer and strengthening facility readiness. Following the Kilifi County training, mentors in Malindi mobilized community health promoters to address fear and awareness barriers among survivors of sexual violence, increasing local knowledge of available services and enhancing community level improvements. Strategic media engagement amplified evidence on contraceptive stock-outs, prompting policy attention. Dialogue with county leaders led to concrete commitments to strengthen post-abortion care and post-rape services.
2. Enhanced social inclusion and well-being: CPSE launched an intervention study that is supporting adolescent mothers in Nairobi's informal settlements with cash transfers, life skills training, and childcare support. CPSE also advanced its work around the inclusion of sexual and gender minorities by strengthening advocacy skills of staff working with civil society organizations in 4 Kenyan counties and influencing public discourse grounded in APHRC evidence. For example, in Rwanda, dialogue workshops involving policymakers, law enforcement, health providers, parents, community leaders, and media actors led parents to acknowledge household stigma and express willingness to adopt more supportive behaviors, including deeper family level engagement to reduce stigma toward sexual and gender minorities communities.
3. Domestication and implementation of SRHR laws, policies and commitment: CPSE evidence shaped national legislation in Sierra Leone, Liberia, and Kenya including contributing to the Kilifi Reproductive, Maternal, Neonatal, Children and Adolescent Health Act (2025). At regional platforms (EAC, AU, SADC), APHRC provided technical input on SRHR bills, gender based violence data systems, the integration of comprehensive sexuality education, harmful practices, and reproductive justice frameworks.
4. Increased evidence demand and use by policy actors: Policy actors actively sought APHRC's expertise to guide lawmaking, policy review, research agenda setting, national survey design, and advocacy messaging. Advisory roles with the WHO, UNDP, SADC, and EAC embedded APHRC within formal decision-making structures. Media professionals and civil society organizations were trained to generate and apply evidence in advocacy, improving the quality of public discourse and institutionalizing data-driven advocacy.
5. Strengthened capacity of civil society partners to advance SRHR programs and advocacy: Youth-led and civil society partners secured new funding (e.g., USD 75,000 for Kilifi youth-led advocacy), institutionalized outcome harvesting, redesigned community programs using CPSE evidence, and enhanced coordination on SRHR policy and financing. These efforts strengthened the sustainability of SRHR advocacy ecosystems across multiple countries.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
